Flatten

/FLAT-uhn/ - rhymes with satin · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Flatten means to make flat or level.

One hailstorm flattened the wheat that a whole dry summer had spared.

Worked Example

Moving day left the family with forty empty boxes and a building rule: nothing goes in the bin until it is flattened. So the kids spent an hour with the box cutter's dull edge, popping tape and pressing each carton down until the tower of cubes became a tidy stack of sheets no taller than a phone book.

Flatten is the exact word for what they did, because flatten means to make flat or level — three dimensions pressed into two. Smooth would only erase the surface's texture and leave the box standing; crush would destroy it entirely. A flattened box survives, just without its height.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

level: Level aims at evenness — a graded road, a floor, a playing field brought to one height. Flatten names a loss instead: whatever had height gives it up entirely. You can level a bumpy lawn and it is still a lawn; flatten a hedge and its shape is gone.

squash: Squash is the informal, kitchen-floor word: flatness produced by sudden force, a grape under a heel. Flatten is calmer and more general — you can flatten a box slowly and neatly, on purpose, and what is flattened survives as a tidy sheet rather than a burst mess.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wrinkle: press creases and ridges back in

crumple: ball it up into folds

Where it sits · how much of the shape is destroyed — smooth → flatten → crush

smooth vs. flatten: Smooth does much less than flatten — it only erases the surface's ridges while the shape underneath keeps its height; flattening presses the whole shape down toward level.

crush vs. flatten: Crush goes further than flatten — a flattened box is still a neat, usable sheet; a crushed one is wreckage.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — flatt

Root — flatt: level, without height (Old Norse flatr; the t doubles before -en)

Suffix — -en

Suffix — -en: to make (as in darken, soften)

Put it together

Put it together: Flatt- (flat, its t doubled before a vowel suffix) + -en (to make) = to make flat. The -en suffix is one of English's oldest verb-makers: put it on an adjective and you get the verb of becoming — darken, soften, widen, flatten. Old Norse flatr sailed in with the Vikings, and English has been pressing things flat with it ever since.

Use the suffix in a new word: embolden

Use the suffix in a new word: embolden: The same -en builds embolden: praise that emboldens a shy student literally makes them bolder, the way a rolling press makes metal flatter.

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Flatten is the plain physical verb, and it names a result: whatever had height loses it. Level aims at evenness — a grade, a floor, a playing field; smooth cares only about texture; squash adds force and haste. In this unit's data talk, flatten also describes curves: a graph that flattens has stopped climbing, its line pressed toward the horizontal.
